abstract.p: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a microvascular complication of diabetes with its exact underlying mechanisms have not been fully elucidated. This study aimed to investigate the effects of key proteins and metabolites on the development of DR. Undiluted vitreous fluid samples were collected from eight patients with proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) and six non-diabetic idiopathic macular hole (iMH) controls. Integration of TMT-tagged quantitative proteomics and untargeted metabolomics analyses was combined with bioinformatics approaches (PCA, differential expression, PPI network, OPLS-DA, pathway enrichment). Key results were validated by ELISA, immunohistochemistry, and cell proliferation and migration assays. Seven key proteins with six key metabolites were identified to be significantly dysregulated in the PDR. In the vitreous body and retinal nerve fiber layer of the DR group, CD5L expression was upregulated, while CLU was downregulated with SERPINF1 (PEDF). CD5L markedly promotes the proliferation and migration of endothelial cells.These molecules were co-enriched in pathways such as the “complement and coagulation cascade” and “prion disease,” suggesting a common mechanism of abnormal vascular permeability, inflammatory response, and microthrombosis. Disturbances in creatine metabolism suggested AMPK-related energy dysregulation, and the interaction between CD5L and microglia emphasized its neuroinflammatory regulatory function. This study revealing biomarkers and therapeutic targets, which provide new ideas for diagnosis and precise intervention.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Diabetic retinopathy (DR), a major microvascular complication of diabetes, is the leading cause of preventable blindness in working-age adults globally1. With the continuous rise in the global prevalence of diabetes, the disease burden of DR is showing unprecedented growth. According to the latest statistics from the International Diabetes Federation (IDF), there are approximately 589 million diabetic patients worldwide, and this number is projected to surge to 853 million by 2050. [Available from: https://idf.org]. This epidemiological trend directly leads to a sharp increase in the number of DR patients, with the latest model projections showing that the global number of DR patients will reach 160 million by 2045, of which approximately 10% will progress to vision-threatening proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) or diabetic macular edema (DME)2.

In terms of pathophysiological mechanisms, the development and progression of DR involve complex multifactorial interactions. Chronic hyperglycemia leads to retinal microvascular endothelial cell damage, pericyte loss, and blood-retinal barrier disruption through mechanisms such as polyol pathway activation, accumulation of advanced glycation end products (AGEs), protein kinase C (PKC) pathway activation, and oxidative stress responses3. Recent studies have further revealed that neuroinflammatory responses and neurovascular unit dysfunction play critical roles in the early stages of DR, manifested by microglial activation, reactive changes in glial cells, and downregulation of neuroprotective factors (e.g. Pigment Epithelium-Derived Factor (PEDF))4. These pathological changes collectively contribute to the characteristic formation of microaneurysms, retinal ischemia-hypoxia, and ultimately pathological neovascularization in DR.

The current clinical treatment strategies mainly include intravitreal injection of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), intravitreal injection of dexamethasone implant, retinal laser photocoagulation, and vitrectomy.5,6. Although these treatments can delay disease progression to some extent, there are still many limitations: some patients respond poorly to anti-VEGF or dexamethasone implant; laser treatment may lead to peripheral visual field defects and nyctalopia; and surgical intervention is only applicable to end-stage cases and cannot reverse existing retinal damage7. More notably, existing treatment modalities primarily target advanced vascular pathologies, while lacking effective interventions for early neurodegenerative changes and metabolic abnormalities, which highlights the urgent need to explore novel mechanisms of DR pathogenesis and develop early intervention strategies.

Recent advances in multi-omics technologies have revolutionized the study of disease mechanisms, particularly in deciphering complex pathological processes such as DR Metabolomics can uncover metabolic alterations in DR by reflecting perturbations in functional metabolic networks8, whereas proteomics can identify differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) in DR, providing direct evidence of disease-related pathways9. Compared with single-omics approaches, the integration of proteomic and metabolomic data enables the reconstruction of protein–metabolite interaction networks and the identification of key cross-omics driving pathways and regulatory nodes, thereby laying the groundwork for precision medicine10,11.

In this study, we performed a combined proteomic and metabolomic analysis of vitreous samples from DR patients to investigate the potential roles and mechanisms of proteins and metabolites in the pathogenesis of DR. By providing a multidimensional perspective on the pathophysiological changes in DR, our research aims to offer new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying DR and to establish a theoretical basis for the development of targeted interventional strategies.

sec.title: 81 deps were identified in DR, involving CLU, SERPINF1, CD5L
sec.p: The Principal Component Analysis (PCA) revealed a clear distinction between the control and DR group samples, with a pronounced clustering of samples within each group (Fig. 1A). This indicated an essentially uniform expression pattern within the groups, reflecting statistically reproducible samples. Furthermore, a total of 81 DEPs were identified between the DR and control groups, with 41 up-regulated and 40 down-regulated in the DR group (Fig. 1B,C). Subsequently, enrichment analyses were conducted to provide preliminary insights into the signaling pathways implicated by the DEPs. Functional enrichment analysis with ClueGO revealed that the DEPs were predominantly enriched in pathways related to the “positive regulation of substrate adhesion-dependent cell spreading”, “complement activation”, and “immunoglobulin complex, circulating” (Fig. 1D). Additionally, the DEPs were significantly enriched in 332 Gene Ontology (GO) entries with 235 biological processes (BPs), 42 cellular components (CCs) and 55 molecular functions (MFs). Among the identified BPs, those associated with candidate genes exhibited a prominent role in “humoral immune response” and “activation of immune response” (Table S1). Meanwhile, the CCs were primarily concentrated within “blood microparticle” and “collagen-containing extracellular matrix”, while the MFs were mainly enriched in “glycosaminoglycan binding” and “enzyme inhibitor activity” (Fig. 1E). The results indicated that DEPs likely played a significant role in immune response mechanisms and the makeup of the extracellular matrix. Moreover, a Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis of the candidate genes revealed the enrichment of 5 pathways, including “complement and coagulation cascades”, “lysosome”, “pertussis”, “staphylococcus aureus infection” and “Cholesterol metabolism”. (Fig. 1F).

sec.title: Top 10 deps revealed distinct subcellular distributions
sec.p: 52 proteins out of 81 DEPs were found to interact in PPI network interactions, such as CLU, FGG and HP (Fig. 2A). The subsequent analysis identified 25 DEPs with betweenness centrality exceeding 10, which were then selected as candidate proteins for further investigation. Among the candidate proteins, the top 10 with the highest betweenness centrality included CLU, CD5L, HP, C5, C4BPA, JCHAIN, PRSS1, PRNP, SERPINF1, and APLP2. Further, subcellular localization analyses were conducted to gain insight into the distribution of the aforementioned 10 candidate proteins within the cells. CLU was ubiquitously distributed within the cell, encompassing locations such as the nucleus, cytoplasm, and microsome. CD5L was observed to localize to both the secreted and cytoplasm. Meanwhile, HP, C5, C4BPA, and JCHAIN were all positioned within the secreted compartment. PRSS1 was distributed in the secreted and extracellular space, while PRNP was located on the cell membrane, lipid-anchor, GPI-anchor, and Golgi apparatus. SERPINF1 was found distributed in both the secreted and melanosome compartments, and APLP2 was distributed across the cell membrane and within the nucleus (Fig. 2B).

sec.p: 2.3 26 differently expressed metabolites (DEMs) were enriched, with most belonging to fatty acyls and carboxylic acids and derivatives.

In the Orthogonal partial least squares-discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA), both the positive and negative ion modes, a distinct differentiation in the relative contents of metabolites was observed between the DR and control groups (Fig. 3A,B), indicating a fundamental similarity in the expression patterns within each group. Afterwards, the DEMs were identified between the DR and control groups. In the positive ion mode, a total of 9 DEMs1 were identified between the DR and control groups, all of which exhibited differential down-regulation in the DR group (Fig. 3C). Conversely, in the negative ion mode, a total of 17 DEMs2 were discerned, with only 4 of these metabolites displaying up-regulation in the DR group, relative to the control (Fig. 3D). Subsequently, a total of 26 DEMs were achieved through the amalgamation of the DEMs1 and DEMs2. Further analysis was conducted on the classification and annotation of DEMs. In the HMDB annotation process, all 26 DEGs were successfully annotated, with the majority (27%) being classified as fatty acyls. The second largest category was that of carboxylic acids and derivatives, which constituted 23% of the total (Fig. 3E). Furthermore, a total of 10 DEMs were annotated and categorized into five distinct categories in the KEGG annotations: carbohydrates, lipids, organic acids, peptides, as well as vitamins and cofactors (Fig. 3F). Of particular note was the lipids category, which encompassed 4 distinct lipid metabolites: fatty acids, prenol lipids, fatty acyls, and polyketides. Notably, the strongest correlation was observed between hexadec-7-enoic acid and 9E-heptadecenoic acid (cor = 0.991, p < 0.0001) (Fig. 3G). This indicated that the metabolic pathways of these two metabolites were closely related, and could be involved in intimately connected biological functions. Further, the DEMs were found to be significantly enriched in the “DNA damage reversal” and “metabolism of carbohydrates” (Fig. 3H). The findings indicated that DEMs could be associated with genomic stability, as well as in energy generation and storage.

sec.title: The correlation of key deps and DEMs indicating CLU, SERPINF1, CD5L and 2-Butyne-1,4-diol in PDR
sec.p: Proteomics and metabolomics association analysis identified 6 key metabolites: Aminooxyacetic acid, Creatine, Methyl ethaneperoxoate, N6-Methyladenosine, Orsellinic acid, and 2-Butyne-1,4-diol, alongside 7 key proteins: Clusterin (CLU), CD5 antigen-like protein (CD5L), C5, serpin family F member 1 (SERPINF1), APLP2, PSAP, and RBP3 (Fig. 4A; Table 1). Remarkably, 2-butyn-1,4-diol demonstrated strong positive correlations with SERPINF1 (cor = 0.873), APLP2 (cor = 0.829), PSAP (cor = 0.855), and RBP3 (cor = 0.846), while exhibiting notable negative correlations with CD5L (cor = -0.895) and C5 (cor = -0.807). In contrast, CLU was positively correlated with all key metabolites, except 2-Butyne-1,4-diol (Fig. 4B).CLU is positively correlated with Aminooxyacetic acid, Creatine, Methyl ethaneperoxoate, N6-Methyladenosine, and Orsellinic acid. SERPINF1 is positively correlated with 2-Butyne-1,4-diol. CD5L is negatively correlated with 2-Butyne-1,4-diol. Furthermore, the DR group exhibited down-regulation of all 6 key metabolites in expression (Fig. 4C, Table S2), while key proteins C5 and CD5L were upregulated (Fig. 4D, Table S3). KEGG pathway analysis of the co-enriched key proteins and metabolites revealed significant enrichment in four pathways: the complement and coagulation cascades, prion diseases, pertussis, and Staphylococcus aureus infection, as visualized in Fig. 4E.

sec.title: The deps and DEMs were confirmed in both clinical and experimental DR
sec.p: Vitreous humor samples from PDR patients (DR group) and iMH patients (Control group) were assayed by ELISA for CD5L, CLU, and SERPINF1. As shown in Fig. 5, CD5L levels were significantly elevated in the DR group compared with controls (p < 0.05), whereas CLU and SERPINF1 concentrations were significantly reduced in the DR group ((p < 0.0001, p < 0.05).

caption.p: ELISA quantification of CD5L (A), CLU (B), and SERPINF1 (C) protein levels in the vitreous humor of DR and Control patients. *p < 0.05, **** p < 0.0001.

sec.p: Paraffin-embedded retinal sections were prepared from streptozotocin-induced diabetic SD rats (DR group) and age-matched non-diabetic controls (Control group) and stained for CD5L, CLU, and SERPINF1. Whole-retina analysis revealed that, compared with controls, DR rats exhibited a significant increase in CD5L immunoreactivity (p < 0.01), while both CLU and SERPINF1 staining were significantly reduced (p < 0.01, p < 0.001). In the retinal nerve fiber layer, cell-specific quantification likewise showed elevated CD5L expression in DR animals (p < 0.01,) and decreased CLU and SERPINF1 levels compared with controls (p < 0.01, p < 0.001).(Fig. 6).

sec.title: Prediction of transcription factors (TFs) and modification sites in key proteins
sec.p: The TFs for key proteins were predicted, with 16, 1, 4, 18, 8, 11, and 2 TFs identified as potential regulators for CLU, CD5L, C5, SERPINF1, APLP2, PSAP, and RBP3, respectively (Fig. 7A). Among them, SERPINF1 predicted the most TFs, including FOXA2, JUND, EBF1. The predictions of modification sites for key proteins indicated that APLP2, RBP3, and SERPINF1 had strong literature support for phosphorylation (Fig. 7B–D), while CLU and PSAP exhibited significant support for acetylation (Fig. 7E,F). C5 was noteworthy for having the most substantial literature support for phosphorylation, acetylation, ubiquitination, and other modifications (Fig. 7G). CD5L was also found to undergo modifications at other sites (Fig. 7H).

sec.title: Drug prediction, molecular docking of key proteins and functional validation
sec.p: A total of 10 potential drugs were predicted for the genes corresponding to the targeted key proteins (Table 2). Among them, RBP3 and vitamin A palmitate exhibited the highest interaction score. In light of the inadequate binding affinity between RBP3 and vitamin A palmitate, a molecular docking was conducted to illustrate the interaction between CD5L and fenoprofen. The CD5L and fenoprofen molecules were showed to dock in Fig. 8A,B. Concurrently, the results of the molecular docking demonstrated that the intermolecular binding energies between CD5L and fenoprofen were determined to be − 6.6 kcal/mol (Table 3). A molecular free energy of ≤ − 1.2 kcal/mol indicated a robust binding affinity between the ligand and the receptor. Therefore, this finding indicated a robust binding affinity between CD5L and fenoprofen.

sec.p: As shown in Fig. 8C, exogenous CD5L intervention markedly promoted the proliferation of C166 cells. This enhancement was confirmed by the EdU assay, showing a statistically significant difference relative to the control group (p < 0.01).
As shown in Fig. 8D, a scratch wound assay demonstrated that exogenous CD5L intervention significantly enhanced the migratory capacity of C166 cells compared to the control group (p < 0.05).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: DR is a progressive and vision-threatening microvascular complication of diabetes, characterized by retinal capillary dysfunction and irreversible structural damage. Its pathogenesis involves a complex interplay of hyperglycemia‑induced metabolic disturbances, endothelial injury, inflammation, oxidative stress, and retinal neurodegeneration12–14. Chronic hyperglycemia and hypertension compromise capillary integrity, leading to increased vascular permeability, ischemia, and pathological neovascularization, which ultimately result in permanent vision loss. In this study, we integrated quantitative proteomics and untargeted metabolomics to identify seven proteins and six metabolites closely associated with DR progression. Correlation analysis and joint pathway enrichment further revealed their convergent roles within key molecular networks. These findings were validated using ELISA and immunohistochemistry, thereby uncovering novel mechanistic insights into DR.

Among the candidate proteins investigated, CD5L is a multifunctional immune modulator secreted primarily by macrophages and belongs to the scavenger receptor cysteine-rich family. CD5L regulates diverse biological processes including apoptosis, pattern recognition, inflammation, autophagy, macrophage polarization, and lipid metabolism15. During inflammatory responses, it plays a key role in modulating macrophage polarization16. At higher concentrations, CD5L has been shown to inhibit HepG2 cell proliferation, suggesting potential antitumor activity17. Although its role in DR remains poorly understood, emerging evidence implicates CD5L in adaptive resistance to anti-angiogenic therapy, possibly through modulation of the vascular or inflammatory microenvironment18.In alignment with these findings, we observed significantly elevated levels of CD5L in the vitreous of patients with PDR and marked upregulation in the nerve fiber layer of DR rat retinas. Under physiological conditions, retinal microglia are predominantly located in the inner plexiform, outer plexiform, and ganglion cell layers19,20. Under hyperglycemic conditions, however, microglia become activated and migrate toward the nerve fiber layer—a spatial pattern consistent with the focal CD5L overexpression detected in our study21,22. Collectively, these observations suggest that CD5L may play a dual role in DR progression, concurrently contributing to both immune regulation and microvascular dysfunction.

CLU is a secreted glycoprotein chaperone present in both intracellular and extracellular fluids, including blood and semen23–25. It functions to inhibit complement activation, regulate immune cell activity, maintain immune tolerance, clear immune complexes, and exert antioxidant effects26. Elevated serum CLU levels have been observed in individuals with obesity and type 2 diabetes, where it correlates with adipose tissue insulin resistance, highlighting its potential as a metabolic biomarker27. In contrast, within the context of DR, hyperglycemia-induced oxidative and inflammatory stress suppresses CLU expression. This downregulation weakens retinal antioxidant defenses and disrupts vascular homeostasis, which is normally maintained in part through modulation of VEGF-driven pathological angiogenesis28,29. Our integrated proteomic and immunohistochemical analyses confirmed a significant reduction in CLU levels, both in the vitreous of patients with PDR and in the retinas of diabetic rats. This tissue-specific dichotomy—systemic elevation versus retinal depletion—underscores the dual role of CLU as both a systemic metabolic regulator and a local protector of retinal integrity.

SERPINF1, a member of the serine protease inhibitor (Serpin) superfamily, encodes pigment epithelium-derived factor (PEDF)—an endogenous inhibitor of Wnt signaling that is abundantly expressed in the vitreous fluid30,31. PEDF helps stabilize the retinal vasculature by antagonizing Wnt pathway activity. In DR, decreased PEDF expression disrupts vascular homeostasis, promoting pathological angiogenesis and enhancing inflammatory responses30. In this study, we detected significant downregulation of SERPINF1 in the vitreous fluid of patients with PDR and in the retinal tissues of diabetic rats, confirming its key inhibitory role in DR pathogenesis. The consistent reduction of SERPINF1 across both clinical and preclinical models highlights its dual potential as a therapeutic target and a biomarker of disease severity. Restoring PEDF levels - for example, through gene therapy or recombinant protein delivery-could simultaneously suppress pathological angiogenesis and neuroinflammation, offering a multi-mechanistic treatment strategy for DR. Creatine, a nitrogenous organic acid endogenously synthesized in vertebrates, acts as a crucial energy buffer in tissues with high metabolic demand, such as neurons and vascular endothelial cells32. In DR, hyperglycemia induced oxidative stress and chronic inflammation disrupt creatine mediated energy homeostasis, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production - key drivers of retinal microvascular damage33. Moreover, creatine metabolism is closely linked to the AMP‑activated protein kinase (AMPK) pathway; dysregulation of creatine metabolism may impair AMPK signaling, further compromising vascular function in DR34. Thus, alterations in creatine metabolism are likely integral to the pathogenesis of DR and may serve as a promising biomarker for early diagnosis.

In the current study, we observed elevated levels of complement C5 in the vitreous humor of patients with PDR. This observation aligns with the fundamental nature of DR as a chronic inflammatory disorder. Aberrant activation of the complement system is a critical component of DR-associated inflammatory cascades. Numerous investigations have shown that both the concentration of C5 protein and the level of its activated fragment C5a are markedly upregulated in the vitreous humor of PDR patients, reflecting robust activation of the local complement system35. Genetic analyses have identified a significant association between the C5-rs17611 polymorphism and DR, specifically susceptibility to PDR, thereby solidifying the role of C5 in DR pathogenesis from a genetic perspective36. Additionally, crosstalk between the complement system (including C5) and retinal resident immune cells, such as microglia, is well established as a key mechanism underlying neurovascular unit impairment in DR37. Collectively, this body of evidence demonstrates that C5 is not a bystander in DR development and progression, but rather an effector molecule implicated in inflammatory amplification, blood-retinal barrier disruption, and neovascularization.

Retinol binding protein 3 (RBP3), also known as Interphotoreceptor Retinoid-Binding Protein (IRBP), is a retinol transporter predominantly expressed by retinal photoreceptors that plays a key role in the visual cycle. In the current study, we observed reduced levels of RBP3 in the vitreous humor of patients with PDR, a finding consistent with results from numerous previous clinical investigations. Studies have confirmed that RBP3 expression is markedly downregulated in both the vitreous humor and retina during the early stages of DR38. Notably, subsequent research has further revealed that higher RBP3 concentrations in the vitreous humor or aqueous humor are significantly associated with milder DR severity, lower levels of inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α) and VEGF, a reduced prevalence of diabetic macular edema (DME), and a decreased risk of DR progression39–41. Mechanistic studies have demonstrated that RBP3 exerts a retinal protective effect by binding to GLUT1 to inhibit glucose uptake and antagonizing the VEGF signaling pathway39. This multi-dimensional evidence from human samples firmly establishes the critical role of RBP3 in DR pathogenesis and supports its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target.

We report for the first time that the level of amyloid precursor-like protein 2 (APLP2) is rEdUced in the vitreous humor of patients with PDR. APLP2 is a key member of the amyloid precursor protein (APP) family and is constitutively expressed in human cerebral vascular endothelial cells42. Structurally homologous to APP770, it contains a Kunitz protease inhibitor (KPI) domain—a motif that has been shown to possess anticoagulant activity by inhibiting coagulation factor function and regulating thrombosis42,43. Furthermore, experimental studies using murine models of type 1 diabetes have demonstrated decreased expression of APP and the α-secretase ADAM10, as well as reduced production of soluble APPα (sAPPα)44. Thus, downregulation of APLP2 may indicate impairment of retinal vascular endothelial function. The reduced APLP2 levels observed in PDR in the present study are likely associated with widespread vascular endothelial dysfunction and impaired neurovascular unit protective mechanisms induced by diabetes, providing a plausible biological explanation for its involvement in DR-associated vascular pathology.

Prosaposin (PSAP) is a multifunctional lysosomal protein and serves as the precursor for four lysosomal activating proteins: Saposins A–D. It is critical for maintaining neuronal survival and synaptic plasticity, regulating lipid antigen presentation and energy metabolism, modulating immune cell function (e.g., the anti-inflammatory and reparative properties of M2 macrophages), and coordinating cell proliferation and apoptosis via signaling pathways such as PI3K/Akt and ERK45. A study analyzing human blood samples identified PSAP as a potential protective factor in DR, noting its significant downregulation in patients with PDR and potential association with the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) and the inflammatory pathology of DR46. In the present study, we observed decreased PSAP levels in the vitreous humor of human PDR patients, which aligns with the protective trend suggested by the aforementioned research. Downregulation of PSAP in PDR may exacerbate damage to the DR neurovascular unit by impairing anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, and tissue repair mechanisms, thereby identifying it as a novel potential target for investigating DR pathogenesis.

It is noteworthy that although the concentrations of CD5L, CLU, and SERPINF1 differed significantly between the PDR and control groups in ELISA, the actual fold-changes were relatively modest. This observation can be explained by several interrelated considerations. (1) Although the absolute changes are not large, they are statistically significant and show consistent directional trends in both clinical (human vitreous) and preclinical (rat retinal tissue) models. In the highly regulated vitreoretinal microenvironment, even subtle dysregulation of key regulatory proteins may lead to functionally important consequences. For instance, a measurable decline in a stabilizing factor such as SERPINF1—even if moderate—could contribute meaningfully to the loss of vascular integrity and neuroprotection in DR. (2) These protein-level changes align with and are supported by our multi-omics findings. The convergence of evidence across proteomic and metabolomic layers enhances the biological plausibility of their role, beyond what concentration differences alone might imply. (3) The vitreous humor is a dynamic fluid whose composition reflects both local retinal pathology and systemic metabolic influences. The modest intergroup differences in CD5L, CLU, and SERPINF1 may therefore represent the integrated outcome of broader physiological regulation, rather than an isolated retinal effect.

A notable finding in this study is the concordant expression pattern of CD5L, CLU, and SERPINF1 between human vitreous (ELISA) and rat retinal tissue (IHC). This cross‑species consistency can be explained by several interrelated factors: (1) Evolutionary Conservation of Pathological Pathways: The regulatory pathways of these proteins are often conserved across species. Consequently, similar disease stimuli—such as those in DR can elicit analogous directional changes in their expression in both humans and rodents17,47. (2) Integrated Response to Retinal Microenvironment Stress: Key stressors in DR (e.g., hyperglycemia, oxidative stress) can coordinately regulate the synthesis, secretion, and degradation of these proteins. For example, CD5L is secreted and acts on neighboring endothelial cells to promote angiogenesis or inflammation. The concomitant rise in its intracellular levels within producing cells suggests a self-reinforcing autocrine/ paracrine loop, a feature common in chronic inflammatory diseases48. Thus, in PDR, diabetes induced stress drives an extracellular increase in CD5L and decreases in CLU and SERPINF1. These changes are not merely passive reflections of disease but likely participate in feedback mechanisms that further modulate intracellular expression, thereby sustaining a cycle of dysregulation within the retinal neurovascular unit.

Due to the limited availability of donated human retinal tissue from our regional eye bank, we were unable to validate the expression of the identified differential proteins directly in human PDR specimens via immunohistochemistry. We acknowledge that direct human tissue validation represents an important step in confirming the clinical relevance of our findings. However, given current ethical and practical constraints—particularly the shortage of suitable PDR samples—such validation was not feasible within the framework of this study. We intend to pursue this line of investigation in future work once ethical approvals and tissue resources become available. In the interim, we utilized a streptozotocin-induced diabetic rat model as a physiologically relevant surrogate to support the experimental validation of our proteomic observations.

Enrichment analysis of DEPs revealed significant enrichment in five key pathways: “Complement and coagulation cascades,” “Lysosome,” “Pertussis,” “Staphylococcus aureus infection,” and “Cholesterol metabolism.” The complement system, as a vital component of innate immunity, plays a critical role in the development and progression of DR49. Studies indicate that aberrant activation of the complement system may contribute to disruption of the NVU, manifesting as vascular cell injury, glial activation, and neuronal dysfunction50. The interaction between the complement system and microglia is particularly prominent in DR. Abnormal microglial activation can exacerbate the complement cascade through the release of inflammatory factors, thereby promoting breakdown of the blood–retinal barrier and neuroinflammation51. Accordingly, targeting the complement system has emerged as a promising therapeutic direction for retinal degenerative diseases, including DR37. The role of the lysosomal pathway in DR is closely associated with microglial function. Retinal microglia, as resident immune cells of the retina, participate in the clearance of metabolic waste and remodeling of the extracellular matrix via lysosomal pathways52. In DR, lysosomal dysfunction may lead to accumulation of metabolic waste such as cholesterol, triggering inflammatory responses and vascular injury53. Furthermore, alterations in lysosome-related gene expression may be linked to the metabolic shift of microglia from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis (M1 polarization), a phenomenon observed in early DR54. To date, no direct association has been established between the pertussis or Staphylococcus aureus infection pathways and DR. Nevertheless, given that pertussis toxin can influence cellular signaling through G protein–coupled receptors, and S. aureus infection may induce systemic inflammation leading to retinal oxidative stress and NVU damage, future studies could explore their potential links with abnormal microglial activation or vascular dysfunction in DR. Dysregulated cholesterol metabolism may represent another mechanism contributing to DR pathogenesis. Cholesterol deposition within the retina can form cholesterol crystals, directly damaging vascular structure and promoting inflammatory responses53. M2-type microglia have been shown to regulate cholesterol metabolism and participate in retinal microangiopathy in DR55.

Protein-metabolite co-enrichment pathway analysis revealed significant enrichment in several key pathways, including “Complement and Coagulation Cascades,” “Prion Diseases,” “Pertussis,” and “Staphylococcus aureus Infection.” Among these, the Complement and Coagulation Cascades pathway is of particular relevance, as it plays a central role in innate immunity and hemostasis. This pathway regulates vascular permeability and microthrombosis through mechanisms such as inflammatory mediator release, pathogen clearance, fibrin deposition, and platelet activation56. In DR, hyperglycemia can activate the complement system, contributing to vascular endothelial injury and breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier. These processes promote retinal ischemia and pathological neovascularization. Furthermore, abnormal activation of the coagulation cascade may exacerbate microvascular thrombosis, which has been linked to vascular leakage and fibrosis in DR57,58.

Common aspects of these pathways in disease include activation of the coagulation cascade and the complement system promoting increased vascular permeability and fibrosis in both DR and infectious diseases56,58. It also allows the complement system, Toll-like receptors and NF-κB pathway56,57 to cross-regulate the inflammatory response in infectious and metabolic diseases, which together promote DR.

A common mechanistic feature shared by these pathways in disease is the activation of both the coagulation cascade and the complement system, which collectively promote increased vascular permeability and tissue fibrosis—a process observed in both DR and certain infectious diseases56,58. Furthermore, these pathways enable cross-talk between the complement system, Toll-like receptors, and the NF-κB pathway56,57, thereby amplifying the inflammatory response in infectious as well as metabolic diseases. Such integrated inflammatory dysregulation is a key driver in the progression of DR.

The present study identifies a novel role for CD5L in stimulating key endothelial cell behaviors- migration and proliferation- that are fundamental prerequisites for angiogenesis59. The enhanced wound closure observed in scratch assays, coupled with increased EdU incorporation, collectively indicates that CD5L shifts endothelial cells toward a more active phenotype. This finding holds particular relevance in the context of DR characterized by progressive retinal vascular dysfunction and pathological neovascularization60. In DR, chronic hyperglycemia and associated metabolic disturbances drive endothelial activation, leading to aberrant vessel growth that underlies much of the disease’s pathology4. Our data suggest that CD5L may contribute to this dysregulated angiogenic response, extending its functional repertoire beyond established roles in immunity and metabolism. It is plausible that CD5L intersects with canonical signaling pathways implicated in both physiological angiogenesis and DR pathogenesis. For instance, CD5L may amplify endogenous VEGF activity- a central driver of retinal neovascularization in DR-or sustain pro-proliferative signals through the ERK or PI3K/Akt pathways, which are frequently upregulated in diabetic endothelial cells61. Whether CD5L expression is altered in the diabetic retina and how it interacts with the hypoxic and inflammatory milieu of DR remain important open questions. Future work should directly evaluate the role of CD5L in DR models, testing its sufficiency to drive capillary tube formation in vitro and pathological neovascularization in vivo, as well as examining its potential as a therapeutic target for mitigating vision loss associated with aberrant angiogenesis.

In this study, an integrated multi‑omics approach combined with in vitro validation (ELISA, immunohistochemistry, cell proliferation assay and migration assay) confirmed the dysregulation of key proteins (CD5L, CLU, SERPINF1) and metabolites (AOAA, creatine) in DR. These findings elucidate their potential pathophysiological roles in DR, providing a foundation for further mechanistic investigation and the development of novel diagnostic markers and therapeutic strategies.

sec.title: Patients and study design
sec.p: This study adhered to the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of Kunming Medical University (Approval No. kmmu20220686). All subjects provided signed consent forms prior to study participation. All experimental protocols involving animals were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the Ethics Committee of Kunming Medical University (Approval No. kmmu20220686).All procedures were performed in strict accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations for the care and use of laboratory animals.This study is reported in full compliance with the ARRIVE (Animal Research: Reporting of In Vivo Experiments) guidelines.

Between March 2025 to May 2025, fourteen patients who underwent pars plana vitrectomy at the Department of Ophthalmology, First Affiliated Hospital of Kunming Medical University, were prospectively recruited. Vitreous samples were divided into two groups: the disease group comprised eight eyes from patients with PDR, and the control group comprised six eyes from nondiabetic patients with idiopathic macular hole (iMH).

Inclusion criteria for the PDR group were: (1) age ≥ 18 years; (2) diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) with PDR requiring vitrectomy for non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage or tractional detachment of retina, DRSS score of 65–85. Inclusion criteria for the control group were: (1) age ≥ 18 years; (2) idiopathic full-thickness macular hole requiring surgical intervention; (3) no history of diabetes (fasting blood glucose < 6.1 mmol/L and HbA1c < 6.0%); and (4) absence of any clinical signs of diabetic retinopathy on fundus examination.

Exclusion criteria for both groups included: (1) vitreous hemorrhage from non-diabetic causes; (2) active ocular inflammation or infection (e.g., blepharitis, dacryocystitis, conjunctivitis, keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis, retinitis); (3) other ocular diseases affecting the posterior segment (e.g., glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration, retinal vasculitis, rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, high myopia); (4) prior intraocular interventions, including laser photocoagulation, intravitreal anti-VEGF or dexamethasone injections, or vitreoretinal surgery; and (5) uncontrolled or untreated systemic conditions such as hypertension, autoimmune or inflammatory disorders, systemic infections, or hematologic diseases.

Undiluted vitreous humor (1.0–1.5 mL) was aspirated at the outset of standard 25-gauge pars plana vitrectomy, before infusion onset, using the vitrector connected to a sterile syringe under low vacuum (< 300 mmHg). Upon collection, samples were placed in ice-cooled microcentrifuge tubes and spun at 3,000 × g (10 min, 4 °C) to pellet cellular debris. The clarified supernatant was then divided into aliquots and frozen at − 80 °C for later proteom.

sec.title: TMT-based proteomics
sec.p: Total protein was extracted in Tris–HCl buffer, and concentration was determined with a microplate reader. Protein integrity was confirmed by SDS–PAGE. For digestion, 150 µg of protein was incubated with sequencing-grade trypsin (Promega, V5280-100 µg) at a 50:1 protein-to-enzyme ratio for 14 h at 37 ℃. Peptides were labeled using the TMT-10plex reagent kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The TMT-labeled peptide samples were combined in equal amounts, mixed with mobile phase A (5% ACN, pH 9.8), and injected into an UltiMate™ 3000 HPLC system (Thermo Scientific) for fractionation. Separation was performed on an Agilent ZORBAX 300Extend-C18 column (4.6 × 150 mm, 3.5 μm) with a linear gradient. The eluted fractions were lyophilized and redissolved in 0.1% FA before nanoLC-MS/MS analysis using an EASY-nLC™ 1200 system connected to an Orbitrap Exploris™ 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in DDA mode. MS parameters included: 2.2 kV spray voltage; MS^1 scans at 120,000 resolution (350–1,500 m/z); 300% AGC target; HCD-based MS^2 at 32% collision energy (45,000 resolution, 110 m/z start); dynamic exclusion of 60 s; precursor charge states 2+–6+; 200% AGC target; 120 ms max injection time. Data were analyzed using MaxQuant (v 2.1.4.0) with Trypsin/P digestion, carbamidomethyl (C) as a fixed modification, and oxidation (M) plus N-terminal acetylation as variable modifications. Database searches employed the UniProt reference proteome, with 1% FDR thresholds for peptides/proteins and exclusion of contaminants/reverse matches.

sec.title: Untargeted lipid metabolomics
sec.p: Each vitreous sample (20 µL) was combined with lipid extraction buffer, incubated for 10 min at room temperature, and kept at − 20 °C overnight. After centrifugation (4,000 × g, 20 min), the clarified supernatant was collected for metabolite profiling. Chromatographic separation was performed on an ACQUITY UPLC system (Waters) equipped with a Kinetex C18 column (100 × 2.1 mm, 100 Å; Phenomenex) maintained at 55 °C (flow rate: 0.3 mL/min). The mobile phases included: (A) ACN/water (60:40, 0.1% FA) and (B) isopropanol/ACN (90:10, 0.1% FA). Metabolite detection was conducted using a Q-Exactive mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific) in dual-polarity mode. Full-scan MS (70–1,050 m/z) was acquired at 70,000 resolution (AGC: 3 × 10^6; max IT: 100 ms), followed by dd-MS/MS (top 3) at 17,500 resolution (AGC: 1 × 10^5; max IT: 80 ms). Data were converted to mzXML and analyzed via XCMS/metaX in R, with features aligned by retention time and m/z.

sec.title: Principal component analysis (PCA) and differential expression analysis
sec.p: To ascertain whether the reproducibility of proteomic sequencing samples was by statistical standards, PCA was conducted on both sample sets utilizing the procmp function from the stats package (v 4.2.2) (https://www.r-project.org/). Moreover, the objective was to identify proteins that exhibited differential expression in the control and DR groups, and DEPs in both groups were identified using the limma package (v 3.54.0)62 (|log2FoldChange (FC)| > 0.5, P < 0.05). Furthermore, the volcano plot and heatmap of DEPs were plotted utilizing the ggplot2 package (v 3.4.1)63 and pheatmap package (v 1.0.12)64, respectively. The top 10 most significantly up- and down-regulated proteins were labelled in the volcano plot (sorted by log2FC value), and the heatmap illustrated their expression profiles.

sec.title: Functional analysis of deps
sec.p: The biological functions of the DEPs were subjected to further analysis. Initially, the molecular function of DEPs was conducted utilising the ClueGO plugin for the Cytoscape software (v 3.9.1)65(P < 0.05). Subsequently, the biological functions of the DEPs were elucidated through the utilization of the clusterProfiler package (v 4.7.1.003)66, which facilitated the performance of GO (P < 0.05) and KEGG enrichment analysis (adj. P < 0.05) on the DEPs. Of which, GO contained 3 parts: BP, (CC, and MF. The GO entries were ordered in descending order of P-values, and displayed the top 3 pathways with the most significant enrichment in BP, CC, and MF, respectively.

sec.title: Identification and subcellular localisation analysis of candidate proteins
sec.p: To investigate the interactions among DEPs, the search tool that retrieves interaction genes (STRING) database (https://www.string-db.org) was employed to generate a protein-protein interaction (PPI) network. The DEPs were imported into the STRING database for the construction of a PPI network (interaction score ≥ 0.4), and the resulting data were subsequently visualized using Cytoscape software (v 3.9.1). Afterwards, the betweenness centrality of DEPs was calculated utilizing the CytoNCA plugin within Cytoscape software (v 3.9.1). Proteins with betweenness centrality values exceeding 10 were selected as candidate proteins. Eventually, subcellular localization analyses of the top 10 candidate proteins, ranked by betweenness centrality, were conducted utilizing the unified protein (UniProt) database (https://www.uniprot.org/) to investigate their distributions within subcellular structures.

sec.title: OPLS-DA
sec.p: The OPLS-DA model was performed to analyze the metabolite profile from disparate sample groups. The variable importance in projection (VIP) values for each metabolite of the control and DR groups from the metabolomic data were calculated using the mixOmics package (v 6.22.0)67 in both positive and negative ion modes for the OPLS-DA models, respectively. A differential expression analysis of metabolome sequencing data, encompassing total samples, was conducted using the limma package (v 3.54.0) in both positive and negative ion modes to ascertain P-values for metabolites between the DR and control groups. Afterwards, incorporating VIP values from the OPLS-DA model, metabolites exhibiting VIP > 1.0 and P < 0.05 were designated as significantly distinct. The process was performed independently for positive and negative ion modes to obtain DEMs1 and DEMs2, which were visualized via volcano plots. Subsequently, DEMs1 and DEMs2 were combined to obtain DEMs after removing duplicates.

sec.title: Functional analysis of DEMs
sec.p: The classification and annotation of DEMs were subjected to further investigation. Initially, the mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) values of the DEMs were imported into the human metabolome database (HMDB) (http://www.hmdb.ca/) to identify the respective metabolite classes. Following this, the DEMs were mapped to the KEGG database (https://www.genome.jp/kegg/) to elucidate their classification. Further explore potential associations between DEMs, based on all samples from metabolome sequencing, a Spearman correlation analysis (|correlation coefficient (cor) | > 0.8 and P < 0.05) was conducted on the DEMs using the corrplot package (v 0.92)68. To elucidate the pathways associated with DEMs, a KEGG metabolic pathway analysis (P < 0.05) was conducted on DEMs via the MetaboAnalyst platform (https://www.metaboanalyst.ca/). The top 20 metabolic pathways of significance were presented as bubble plot.

sec.title: Proteomics and metabolomics association analysis
sec.p: To identify key proteins and key metabolites, all samples from proteomic and metabolomic sequencing data were integrated, and Spearman correlation coefficients were computed between candidate proteins and DEMs utilizing the corrplot package (v 0.92). Furthermore, a heatmap of the correlation between candidate proteins and DEMs was plotted using the ComplexHeatmap package (v 2.14.0)69. Candidate proteins and DEMs with |cor| > 0.8 and P < 0.05 were considered to be strongly correlated, consequently identified as key proteins and key metabolites. Subsequently, the interaction network between key proteins and key metabolites was visualized using Cytoscape software (v 3.9.1) to elucidate their interconnections. The expression of key metabolites and key proteins in both the control and DR groups was further illustrated utilizing the ggplot2 package (v 3.4.1). Thereafter, the KEGG metabolic pathway analysis (adj. P < 0.05) of the key proteins and key metabolites was conducted using the MetaboAnalyst platform, which revealed their co-enriched biological functions.

sec.title: TFs prediction and protein post-translational modifications analysis of key proteins
sec.p: The chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) data from the chromatin enrichment analysis database 3 (ChEA3) (https://maayanlab.cloud/chea3/) was utilized to predict TFs that potentially target these key proteins, thereby facilitating a deeper understanding of the regulatory mechanisms governing these key proteins. Besides, the post-translational modifications analysis of key proteins was conducted, which revealed intricate mechanisms underlying their functional regulation through chemical modifications, such as phosphorylation and acetylation, that occur after translation. The potential modification sites on key proteins were retrieved from the PhosphoSitePlus database (https://www.phosphosite.org/homeAction.action) upon inputting their names, thereby facilitating insights into protein function and regulatory mechanisms.

sec.title: Potential drug prediction and molecular docking of key proteins
sec.p: The “approved” drugs with the potential to target genes corresponding to key proteins were identified through the drug-gene interaction database (DGIdb) (https://www.dgidb.org/). The drug exhibiting the highest gene interaction score corresponding to the key protein was selected as a candidate drug. Subsequently, molecular docking of candidate drugs and key proteins was performed. The candidate drugs were imported into the Public Chemistry Database (PubChem) (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) to obtain their 3D structures. Following this, the key proteins were subjected to molecular docking with the drug candidate utilizing the CB-Dock2 online tools (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/), and the resulting free binding energies were evaluated. Eventually, the results of the molecular docking were visualised using PyMOL software (v 3.0.3)70.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed in R (version 4.2.2), with group comparisons assessed by the Wilcoxon test (significance threshold: p < 0.05).

sec.title: Quantification of CD5L, CLU, and SERPINF1 in vitreous humor by enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
sec.p: Vitreous samples (150 µL) collected from PDR patients and controls (see Sect. 4.1.1) were assayed for CD5L, CLU, and SERPINF1 using commercially available ELISA kits (CD5L: LY0561-HA; CLU: LY1452-A; SERPINF1: LY0563-HA; all from Enzyme-Linked, Jiangsu, China). Samples and standards (150 µL each) were added to precoated 96-well plates (50 µL per well), mixed gently, and sealed with plate film. Plates were incubated at 37 °C for 30 min. After removing the film, wells were emptied, patted dry, and washed five times with 200 µL wash buffer (30 s per wash). Next, 50 µL of horseradish peroxidase–conjugated detection antibody was added to each well, plates were resealed and incubated at 37 ℃ for 30 min, then washed once. For color development, 50 µL each of substrate solutions A and B were added sequentially, mixed by gentle tapping, and incubated in the dark at 37 ℃ for 10 min. The reaction was stopped with 50 µL stop solution, and optical density at 450 nm was measured within 15 min using a BioTek ELx800 microplate reader. Data were analyzed by one-way ANOVA with post hoc t-test comparisons in GraphPad Prism.

sec.title: Immunohistochemical analysis of CD5L, CLU, and SERPINF1 in retinal sections
Animal model and tissue harvest
sec.p: Fifteen male Sprague–Dawley rats (6–8 weeks old, weighing 250–280 g) were obtained from Henan Skebes Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (SCXK [Yu] 2020-0005; SYXK [Dian] K2020-0006). Diabetic retinopathy was induced in the experimental group by intraperitoneal injection of streptozotocin (STZ; 45 mg/kg; Solarbio, S8050) for five consecutive days. Controls received equal volumes of citrate buffer (Solarbio, C1013). Blood glucose was measured on days 2 and 7 post-final injections and weekly thereafter; rats with sustained glucose > 16.7 mmol/L were considered diabetic. At the time of euthanasia, the body weight of rats in the control group ranged from 400 to 420 g, whereas rats in the DR group exhibited a markedly lower weight range of 210 to 230 g. Four weeks post-model induction, rats were euthanized via an overdose of sodium pentobarbital (2%) administered intraperitoneally at a dose of 100 mg/kg. Death was confirmed by the absence of thoracic and abdominal movements, loss of the blink reflex upon gentle corneal touch, and lack of a withdrawal response to a firm toe pinch. Eyeballs were enucleated, embedded in OCT compound, and frozen. Retinal blocks were sectioned at 5 μm on a cryostat, mounted on cationic slides, air-dried in 20% ethanol, then floated on a 47 ℃ water bath, and finally baked at 64 ℃ until the tissue adhered firmly.

sec.title: Paraffin embedding and sectioning
sec.p: Retinal tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24–48 h, washed in PBS, and dehydrated through graded ethanol (75%, 4 h; 85%, 2 h; 90%, 2 h; 95%, 60 min; 100% I, 30 min; 100% II, 30 min). Samples were cleared in xylene (I, 8 min; II, 8 min), then infiltrated in molten paraffin (I, 60 min; II, 60 min; III, 60 min). Tissue blocks were embedded in paraffin molds and allowed to solidify. Paraffin blocks were trimmed and sectioned at 3 μm on a rotary microtome (Leica RM2135), floated on 20% ethanol, transferred to a 47 ℃ water bath, and mounted on cationic slides. Slides were dried in a 64 ℃ oven until paraffin melted and tissue adhered.

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry
sec.p: Slides were baked at 64 ℃ for 1 h, deparaffinized in xylene (I, 10 min; II, 10 min), rehydrated through graded alcohols (100% I, 5 min; 100% II, 5 min; 95%, 5 min; 80%, 3 min; 70%, 2 min), and rinsed in PBS (3 × 5 min). Antigen retrieval was performed in citrate buffer under pressure for 3 min, followed by cooling and PBS washes (3 × 5 min). Endogenous peroxidase was quenched with 3% H2O2 for 20 min at room temperature, then blocked with 5% bovine serum albumin at 37 ℃ for 30 min. Primary antibodies—anti-CD5L (1:50; Bioss, bs-2487R), anti-CLU (1:50; Bioss, bs-1354R), and anti-SERPINF1 (1:50; Bioss, bs-20784R)—were applied overnight at 4 ℃. Slides were warmed to 37 ℃ for 30 min the next day, washed in PBS (3 × 5 min), and incubated with signal enhancer (100 µL) at 37 ℃ for 20 min. After PBS washes, slides were incubated with polymerized goat anti-mouse/rabbit IgG–HRP (1:200; PV-9000; Zhongshan Golden Bridge, Beijing) at 37 ℃ for 20 min, followed by PBS washes. DAB substrate (ZLI-9019; Zhongshan Golden Bridge) was applied until the optimal color was developed, then rinsed in PBS. Counterstaining was performed with hematoxylin for 5 min, differentiated briefly, rinsed in running water for 15 min, dehydrated through graded alcohols and xylene, and mounted with neutral resin. Whole-slide images were acquired on an SQS-12P scanner (Johnson & Johnson, Shenzhen). Quantification of positive staining was performed in ImageJ Pro-Plus, and statistical analyses were conducted in GraphPad Prism.

sec.title: Effect of CD5L on proliferation and migration of vascular endothelial cells
Cell culture
sec.p: The C166 mouse endothelial cell line was obtained from ORICells (Shanghai, China; ORC1034). Cells were maintained in high-glucose Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (high-glucose DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), at 37℃ in a humidified 5% CO2 atmosphere. For routine culture, cells were passaged at 80–90% confluence by washing with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), detaching with 0.25% trypsin-EDTA for approximately 3 min at 37℃, and neutralizing the digestion with complete medium. After centrifugation at 1000 rpm for 5 min, the pellet was resuspended and seeded into fresh flasks at a 1:2 or 1:3 split ratio. Medium was changed every 24–48 h.

sec.title: EdU assay
sec.p: Two groups of C166 cells in good condition and at approximately 80% confluence were refreshed with complete high-glucose DMEM. The C166 + CD5L group was supplemented with 400 pg/mL recombinant CD5L protein (MCE, USA, HY-P72717), while the control group received an equal volume of PBS. Cells were then incubated at 37 °C under 5% CO2 for 24 h. Cell proliferation was assessed using the BeyoClick™ EdU-488 kit (Beyotime, China; C0071). After the respective treatments, cells were incubated with 10µM EdU working solution (prepared by diluting the EdU stock in complete high-glucose DMEM) for 2 h at 37 °C under 5% CO2. Following EdU labeling, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min at room temperature and then permeabilized. After washing with PBS, a Click reaction mixture—prepared from Click Reaction Buffer, CuSO4, Azide 488, and Click Additive Solution as per the manufacturer’s instructions—was added to each well and incubated for 30 min in the dark. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI for 5 min. Following final washes, the cells were imaged under a fluorescence microscope. Proliferation rates were evaluated based on the proportion of EdU-positive cells.

sec.title: Scratch wound assay
sec.p: C166 cells were seeded into 12‑well plates at a density of 1 × 105 cells per well and cultured until reaching 90–95% confluence. Two perpendicular, straight scratches were made in each well using a sterile 200 µL pipette tip, with a distance of 4–6 mm between scratches. After scratching, the medium was gently aspirated and the monolayer was washed once with PBS to remove detached cells. Then, 1 mL of complete high‑glucose DMEM was added to each well. The C166 + CD5L group was supplemented with 400 pg/mL recombinant CD5L protein, while the control group received an equal volume of PBS. The plates were immediately placed under a microscope, and images of the scratches were captured at marked positions as the 0 h reference. Cells were subsequently incubated at 37 °C under 5% CO2. At 24 h and 48 h post‑scratching, the medium was replaced with fresh complete medium, and images were taken again at the same marked locations. Cell migration rates were quantified by measuring the changes in scratch width at 0 h, 24 h, and 48 h.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Through an integrated proteomic and metabolomic approach, this study identified seven key proteins (CLU, CD5L, C5, SERPINF1, APLP2, PSAP, RBP3) and six key metabolites (aminooxyacetic acid, creatine, methyl ethaneperoxoate, N6-methyladenosine, orsellinic acid, 2-butyne-1,4-diol) that are associated with DR. Experimentally, we confirmed that the levels of CD5L was significantly elevated, whereas CLU, SERPINF1 were significantly reduction in the vitreous humor of DR patients compared with controls. These findings were further corroborated in a DR rat model, where immunohistochemistry demonstrated that the expression trends of all three proteins in the rat retinal nerve fiber layer aligned with their concentration levels in human vitreous humor. We conducted in vitro cell experiments and verified that CD5L significantly promoted the proliferation and migration of endothelial cells. These findings suggest that CD5L—identified as a differential protein through proteomic screening—may play a pro‑angiogenic role in the progression of PDR and could represent one of the key proteins involved in the development and advancement of PDR. However, this study has several limitations. One limitation of this study is the absence of direct immunohistochemical validation of the identified proteins in human PDR tissues, due to constrained availability of donated retinal samples from the regional eye bank. Therefore, validation was performed using a streptozotocin‑induced diabetic rat model as a surrogate. Future studies will aim to verify these findings in human tissues once suitable samples and ethical approvals are obtained. Another limitation of our study is that, while we have identified CD5L can promote angiogenesis in PDR, we have not yet performed functional validation of its associated drug candidate, fenoprofen. Further investigation into the pharmacological effects of fenoprofen on CD5L-mediated pathways represents a promising research direction. Future studies will focus on this aspect to explore potential therapeutic strategies for PDR. Moreover, the limitation of this study is the restricted vitreous sample size and the inherent differences between rodent models and human DR. Future research should validate these candidates in larger clinical cohorts, utilize genetic models to establish causal roles (e.g., CD5L), and evaluate combined metabolic and immunomodulatory therapies. These steps are essential for translating these findings into clinically relevant strategies.
